sections.overview: Astyanax jordani is the name commonly applied to a blind cave-dwelling Mexican tetra, though some taxonomies treat cave fish as Astyanax mexicanus populations.
sections.identification: Adults are small, pale and lack functional eyes; the cave form contrasts with eyed, pigmented surface tetras assigned to the closely related A. mexicanus.
sections.habitat: The recognized cave form comes from subterranean freshwater systems in northeastern Mexico, where populations occupy separate limestone caves rather than open rivers.
sections.diet: Species-level field diet data are limited; cave populations of the Mexican tetra lineage exploit food reaching underground waters, but exact prey proportions for A. jordani remain unverified.
sections.behavior: Without vision, these fish navigate in perpetual darkness using nonvisual senses; comparative experiments found that cave and surface forms retain broad hearing ability.
sections.reproduction: FishBase reports adhesive eggs scattered among crevices, which can hide them from parents and other cave inhabitants; detailed reproductive observations remain scarce.
sections.ecology: Its cave form is a striking example of sensory and developmental change within the Mexican tetra complex, while nearby surface populations retain eyes and pigmentation.
sections.conservation: FishBase reports an Endangered global assessment for A. jordani, and Mexican researchers have warned that groundwater extraction and unprotected cave habitats threaten blind cavefish.
